stem: A client with chronic kidney disease asks whether everyone with CKD should follow the same low-potassium, low-phosphorus, high-protein diet. Which response is best?

options.A: Restrict potassium and phosphorus to the same low targets for every person with CKD regardless of laboratory results or disease stage.
options.B: Increase protein substantially for every person with CKD, including people who are not receiving dialysis or losing protein.
options.C: Avoid nutrition modifications because dietary sodium, potassium, phosphorus, protein, and fluid intake do not affect CKD management.
options.D: Individualize sodium, potassium, phosphorus, protein, and fluid goals to kidney function, laboratory results, treatment status, and nutrition needs.

rationale: NIDDK states that there is no single meal plan for everyone with CKD and that nutritional needs change as kidney disease advances. Potassium, phosphorus, protein, sodium, and fluid recommendations depend on kidney function, blood-test results, dialysis/treatment status, and nutritional needs. For example, some people with CKD may need moderate protein, whereas people receiving dialysis may need more protein. D is correct.
educational_objective: Individualize CKD nutrition recommendations to kidney function, laboratory values, treatment/dialysis status and overall nutrition rather than using universal potassium, phosphorus, protein or fluid targets.
source_organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
source_document_title: Healthy Eating for Adults with Chronic Kidney Disease
source_locator: Why is healthy eating important? nutritional needs change as CKD advances. Nutrient-specific sections: fluid depends on kidney function; potassium goal should be individualized with labs; phosphorus may need adjustment based on blood levels; protein amount should be individualized and dialysis may increase protein needs; sodium limit depends on kidney health. How can I eat healthy with CKD?: no single meal plan for everyone with CKD.
source_claim_supported: CKD dietary goals are individualized rather than universal; sodium, potassium, phosphorus, protein and fluid needs vary with kidney function, laboratory findings, treatment/dialysis and nutritional status.

correction_summary: Retained key D and the individualized-CKD-nutrition construct, refined 'stage' to kidney function plus laboratory/treatment/nutrition context, explicitly accounted for different protein needs on dialysis, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.exact_locator: NIDDK no-single-meal-plan and nutrient-specific sections; NCSBN Basic Care p.11 screenshot verified
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item accurately avoids universal potassium/phosphorus/protein restrictions and ties nutrition goals to kidney function, labs and treatment status.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because potassium/phosphorus restrictions depend on individual status and laboratory values.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because high protein is not appropriate for every CKD patient; needs differ, including dialysis status.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because diet and fluid intake are important components of CKD management.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D reflects NIDDK's individualized approach across the named nutrients/fluids.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives are CKD dietary strategies and require individualized-management knowledge.
audit_findings.blueprint: Basic Care and Comfort — nutrition and intake/output assessment.
